what: A real consumer's Python contract, as a script profile's `python` section, vendored so OAIY
can prove that a host holding ONLY the profile builds the right project and reports the
author's own line numbers — without depending on that consumer's repository.
This is the shape the widening exists for. Before `modes`, a profile could carry one file set,
one entry and one call; this contract has FIVE entry modules, two of which are the two phases
of one evaluation, each with its own wrapper and its own line arithmetic. A profile that could
not say that validated perfectly and was useless to anyone but the product that wrote it.
OAIY names nothing in here. Every file name, every wrapper, every offset and the contract id
are the requester's, and they appear in this fixture and in the test that reads it — never in
`zipp-script.ts`, the schemas or a refusal message.

The `syntax` mode's entry defines `__formlogic_compiled__`, not `__formlogic_run__`, because a
syntax check is meant to compile the block and run nothing. The project compiles every module
something imports even from a function that is never reached, so the `import logic_block` lives

imported the block would make the check run the code it is checking. That is why the mode carries
its own `call`: without one, the only signal of success would be the shared call failing.

# formlogic-python/1 entry: an app-logic script. The value is run(ctx)'s return, None when
# the script defines no run.
import formlogic as _fl


def __formlogic_run__(ctx):
    import logic_block
    run = getattr(logic_block, "run", None)
    return _fl._plain(run(ctx)) if callable(run) else None

# formlogic-python/1 entry: a syntax check - does the author's block COMPILE?
#
# The compile IS the check, and the project does it: ZIPP compiles every project module
# something in the project imports, even from a function that never runs (an import that is
# never reached still names the module), and it EXECUTES a module only when an import of it
# actually runs. So a block that does not parse fails while the project is being set up, with
# a `source` error on the author's own line; a block that parses leaves nothing left to check;
# and in neither case has a statement of the block run. The import at the foot of this module
# is what makes that true - delete it and every block compiles clean - so a corpus case pins it.
#
# Which is why the function a caller reaches is NOT the one that imports it. FormLogic's own
# host calls nothing here - it builds the project and stops - but a consumer unfolding the
# served profile calls this mode's `call` as it calls every other mode's, and an
# `import logic_block` in THAT function would execute the author's top level: a syntax check
# with side effects, which is the one thing this mode exists not to have. The import therefore
# lives where it is compiled and never run, and the call answers the same None the host does.
def __formlogic_compiled__():
    return None


def _compiles_logic_block():
    import logic_block

the condition wrapper has the expression wrapper's offset and the same splice-line answer
